claims.text: Postmortem 0001 is the incident incident-drill.sh reproduces on staging, written as if for a real incident; its contributing factors include a configuration change that skipped the canary ADR 0019 requires for api.

Psychological safety: a team's shared belief that a person can admit a mistake, ask a question or raise a problem without being punished or shamed; blameless-culture.md lines 5-8 name this as the goal of the leaders' commitments.

blameless-culture.md lines 3-8: the blameless postmortem template is not enough; if a leader asks who did it after an incident, people learn to hide what they know and the next postmortem finds less; leaders = team lead, product owner, direct manager, committing in front of everyone.

blameless-culture.md lines 12-19: postmortems and incident counts never judge a person; the first reporter is thanked before the team even if they caused it; ask what allowed it, not who; 0001 is the example (unwritten canary rule, reasonable ground, process fix).
Postmortem 0001's action item to write into canary-checks.md that api configuration changes also go through the canary is owned by the team lead (a role), not by the person who made the commit.

blameless-culture.md lines 23-30: responsibility remains: each person keeps their action items until done (like the owner column), tells their part of the review (saw, did, why reasonable); a repeated behaviour is handled privately by the direct manager, outside the postmortem.
blameless-culture.md lines 34-36: the four delivery metrics describe the delivery system, not individuals, and are not used to rank anyone; the same holds for incident and postmortem counts.

delivery-metrics.md lines 60-64: used to rank developers, people tune the number instead of the system, e.g. not writing incident records; lines 46-47, 66: the team reads trends over quarters, with that quarter's incident records.

blameless-culture.md lines 40-48: each quarter the team lead checks signs: fewer near misses reported while deploys do not fall; an incident shops find first; shorter postmortems; a sign goes to the next retrospective as a team problem, not a hunt for the silent.

What people report next depends on how leaders react in public after a mistake, not only on the template (lines 3-5: the template is not enough); each safe reaction makes the next report more likely; one 'who did it?' can undo what the template asks for.

Trade-offs: public blame never fits a mistake; template-only blameless and nobody-responsible fit rarely (the gaps the document names); the document's choice holds only while leaders keep it after costly incidents too.

Choices: a second incident by the same developer still gets 'what allowed it', a pattern goes privately to the direct manager; refuse per-developer incident counts, offer the four delivery metrics as trends; a drop in near misses goes to the retrospective, not good news.

Symptoms (hedged): action items open for sprints with no owner; postmortems shorter with fewer factors while the template is unchanged; shops find an incident before the team; a falling report count can mean people stopped speaking.
Try it: 1 keeps (lines 13-14); 2 breaks (line 12, 34-36); 3 keeps (25-26; lines 18-19 aim action items at the process, not a person); 4 breaks (15); 5 breaks (29-30).
on-call-staffing.md lines 29-30, 39-40: each month the team lead counts per-person on-call load; the counts are used only to share load, never to rate anyone.

beyond_scope: Section 5 notes postmortem 0001's action-item owner is a role (team lead); section 7 cites delivery-metrics.md on reading trends with incident records.
